summary.title: Engineers Do Not Get To Make Startup Mistakes When They Build Ledgers
summary.one_liner: Learn why single-entry bookkeeping breaks in fintech and how to design a double-entry ledger using Accounts, Entries, and Transactions with pending/posted states and normal balances.
takeaways: Single-entry ledgers can show money flows but not why they happened, which makes discrepancies like lost cents hard to debug.
A double-entry ledger is built from three entities: Accounts, Entries (always paired), and Transactions that enforce pairing.
Entries start as pending and can be discarded or posted; discarding keeps history cleaner than reversal entries.
Use normal credit/debit balances on accounts instead of signed amounts on entries.
Sagas trade atomicity for availability, which fits Transactions that may partially fail and need compensating entries.
summary.summary: The author recounts how a stock trading startup skipped double-entry accounting and ended up with unexplained few-cent discrepancies that users noticed and support had to fix manually. The article then explains the conceptual model of a double-entry ledger: the difference between balance-as-property and a separate ledger data model, the Accounts/Entries/Transactions entities, entry statuses (pending, discarded, posted), normal balances instead of negative numbers, and how Sagas fit partial failures. It closes with a list of external references on ledger engineering and a request for reader interest in a future book.
